title: Block close: the long story
hookLine: from Joshua to Lagos, saints and sinners, and the thread holding

cards: Line them up, the way this year met them. Joshua at the edge of the river, told to be strong and courageous. Ruth gleaning at the edge of a field.
Elijah on Carmel. Ignatius in chains on the road to Rome. Francis kissing a leper.
Luther hidden in the Wartburg. Harriet Tubman going back, and back again. Bonhoeffer in a cell.
Mahalia Jackson singing. A young woman in Lagos leading a choir. The year didn't hide the other faces: the burnings, the betrayals, the abuse.

teach.h: A ROLL CALL WITH SAMSON IN IT.
teach.b: The letter to the Hebrews has a roll call too. Chapter eleven names people who lived by faith: Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab.
Then it speeds up, and the names get uncomfortable: "Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae". Samson, whose story is full of violence and bad choices. Jephthah, who made a terrible vow.
Hebrews doesn't scrub them. It puts them in the line.
Then it says something honest about all of them: they "received not the promise". They died before they saw how it ended.

Chapter twelve turns to the reader: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight". A stadium, with the ones who ran before in the stands.
That's what this year has been: a cloud of witnesses, flawed and faithful. But Hebrews does not say the thread is them.
The next verse tells the runner where to look: "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith".

teach.h: THE SAME YESTERDAY, TO DAY, FOR EVER.
teach.b: And near the end: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever." That's the claim Hebrews makes about the long story. The heroes don't hold it together; some of them nearly pulled it apart.
What holds, in Hebrews, is the one the runners look toward, and in that reading he is the same at the river with Joshua and in a classroom church in Lagos.
Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants would tell parts of this year's story differently, and some in it fought each other. Hebrews still puts the runner's eyes in one place.

how: Christians remember those who went before them in sermons, hymns, saints' days and family stories, sometimes reading Hebrews 11 and 12 on the 'cloud of witnesses'.

"so great a cloud of witnesses... let us run with patience the race."

games.q: you're running a long race, and the stands are full of those who ran before you. Hebrews says lay aside every weight. where does it tell you to look?
o: at the crowd in the stands.
back at the runners behind you.
unto Jesus, the author and finisher of your faith.
games.why: Hebrews 12:2. the witnesses matter, but they aren't the thread. the runner is told to look past them, to Jesus.

practice: Let the faces of this year pass by slowly, the prophets, the monks, the reformers, the singers, the nurses, the martyrs, the ones who failed, until one of them stays a little longer than the others.
If you pray, you can give thanks for that life; if you don't, just hold the name with respect.

wordCard.voice: Witnesses. Hebrews' name for all who ran before, named in a cloud, pointing the runner's eyes not to themselves but to Jesus.

carryVoice: Your line: the thread holds. Tomorrow a new block begins, a year of feasts and saints' days. This block, closed.
